claim: The amino acid sequences of CLV3 and CLE40 differ at 4 out of 13 positions.
source: The amino acid sequences of CLV3 and CLE40 differ at 4 out of 13 positions (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly stated in text and supported by Figure 1A showing sequence alignment

claim: CLE40 expression from the CLV3 promoter can fully complement a clv3-2 mutant.
source: Previous studies showed that CLE40 expression from the CLV3 promoter can fully complement a clv3-2 mutant, indicating that CLE40 can substitute CLV3 function in the shoot meristem to control stem cell homeostasis, if expressed from the stem cell domain.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous studies

claim: CLV3 and CLE40 genes carry two introns at very similar positions.
source: Furthermore, while all other CLE genes in Arabidopsis lack introns, the CLE40 and CLV3 genes carry two introns at very similar positions (Hobe et al., 2003), indicating close evolutionary relatedness.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hobe et al., 2003

claim: CLV3 and CLE40 locate in the same phylogenetic cluster together with CLV3 orthologues from rice, maize and tomato.
source: Phylogenetic analysis revealed that CLV3 and CLE40 locate in the same cluster together with CLV3 orthologues from rice, maize and tomato (Goad et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Goad et al., 2017

claim: In clv3-9 mutants, meristem areas increased to ~450% of wild-type (Col-0) levels.
source: In clv3-9 mutants, meristem areas increased to ~450% of wild-type (Col-0) levels, while shoot meristems from four independent cle40 mutant alleles in a Col-0 background (cle40-2, cle40-cr1, cle40-cr2, cle40-cr3) reached only up to 65% of wild type (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).
evidence: Quantitative data from measurements shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C

claim: Shoot meristems from four independent cle40 mutant alleles reached only up to 65% of wild type.
source: In clv3-9 mutants, meristem areas increased to ~450% of wild-type (Col-0) levels, while shoot meristems from four independent cle40 mutant alleles in a Col-0 background (cle40-2, cle40-cr1, cle40-cr2, cle40-cr3) reached only up to 65% of wild type (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).
evidence: Quantitative data from measurements shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C

claim: Carpel number was 2 ± 0.0 (N = 290) in Col-0 and cle40-2 (N = 290) but 3.7 ± 0.4 (N = 340) in clv3-9.
source: Next, we used carpel number as a rough proxy for flower meristem (FM) size, which was 2 ± 0.0 (N = 290) in Col-0 and cle40-2 (N = 290) but 3.7 ± 0.4 (N = 340) in clv3-9 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Quantitative data from carpel counting shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: CLE40 mainly promotes IFM growth, whereas CLV3 serves to restrict both IFM and FM sizes.
source: Hence, we concluded that CLE40 mainly promotes IFM growth, whereas CLV3 serves to restrict both IFM and FM sizes.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the carpel number and meristem size data presented

claim: CLE40 is expressed in IFMs and FMs, starting at P5 to P6 onwards.
source: CLE40 is expressed in IFMs and FMs, starting at P5 to P6 onwards (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Observed expression pattern shown in Figure 2A–C using CLE40:Venus-H2B reporter

claim: CLE40 expression is stronger in the PZ than in the CZ.
source: We found stronger expression in the PZ than in the CZ, and no expression in young primordia.
evidence: Observed from reporter line expression patterns

claim: CLE40 is not expressed in the CZ, and only occasionally in the OC region.
source: Longitudinal optical sections through the IFM showed that CLE40 is not expressed in the CZ, and only occasionally in the OC region (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-E').
evidence: Observed expression pattern from confocal microscopy images

claim: CLE40 expression is lacking at sites of primordia initiation (P0 to P4/5).
source: Expression of CLE40 changed dynamically during development: expression was concentrated in the IFM, but lacking at sites of primordia initiation (P0 to P4/5, Figure 2C).
evidence: Observed expression pattern from confocal microscopy images

claim: In older primordia from P5/6 onwards, CLE40 expression is detectable from the centre of the young FM and expands towards the FM periphery.
source: In older primordia from P5/6 onwards, CLE40 expression is detectable from the centre of the young FM and expands towards the FM periphery.
evidence: Observed expression pattern from reporter line

claim: CLE40 is lacking in young sepal primordia (P6), but starts to be expressed on the adaxial sides of petals at P7.
source: In the FMs, CLE40 is lacking in young sepal primordia (P6), but starts to be expressed on the adaxial sides of petals at P7 (Figure 2A, P1–P7).
evidence: Observed expression pattern from confocal microscopy images

claim: CLV3 and CLE40 are expressed in almost mutually exclusive domains of the IFM, with CLV3 in the CZ surrounded by CLE40 expressing cells.
source: CLV3 and CLE40 are expressed in almost mutually exclusive domains of the IFM, with CLV3 in the CZ surrounded by CLE40 expressing cells (Figure 2D–F'', Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Observed from double reporter line CLE40:Venus-H2B;CLV3:NLS-3xmCherry

claim: In the deeper region of the IFM, where the OC is located, both CLV3 and CLE40 are not expressed.
source: In the deeper region of the IFM, where the OC is located, both CLV3 and CLE40 are not expressed (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Observed from double reporter line expression patterns

claim: CLE40 is downregulated where WUS is expressed, or where WUS protein localizes, such as the OC and CZ.
source: We noted that CLE40 is downregulated where WUS is expressed, or where WUS protein localizes, such as the OC and CZ.
evidence: Inference from comparing CLE40 and WUS expression patterns

claim: CLE40 is lacking in very early flower primordia and incipient organs.
source: Furthermore, CLE40 is also lacking in very early flower primordia and incipient organs.
evidence: Observed from reporter line expression patterns

claim: In clv3-9 mutants, WUS is no longer repressed by the CLV signalling pathway, and the CZ of the meristem increases in size.
source: In clv3-9 mutants, WUS is no longer repressed by the CLV signalling pathway, and the CZ of the meristem increases in size as described previously (Clark et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Clark et al., 1995 and observed phenotype

claim: In clv3-9 mutant meristems, both CLV3 and WUS promoter activity is found in an expanded domain.
source: In the clv3-9 mutant meristems, both CLV3 and WUS promoter activity is now found in an expanded domain (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observed from reporter line expression in clv3-9 background

claim: In clv3-9 mutants, CLE40 is not expressed in the tip and centre of the IFM but is rather confined to the peripheral domain, where neither CLV3 nor WUS are expressed.
source: CLE40 is not expressed in the tip and centre of the IFM but is rather confined to the peripheral domain, where neither CLV3 nor WUS are expressed (Figure 3B', Figure 3—figure supplement 1B').
evidence: Observed from CLE40 reporter in clv3-9 background

claim: CLV3:WUS misexpression triggers a positive feedback loop resulting in continuous enlargement of the CZ.
source: Since WUS activates the CLV3 promoter, CLV3:WUS misexpression triggers a positive feedback loop. This results in a continuous enlargement of the CZ (Brand et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brand et al., 2002

claim: Young seedlings carrying the CLV3:WUS transgene at 10 days after germination (DAG) displayed a drastically enlarged SAM compared to wild-type seedlings of the same age.
source: Young seedlings carrying the CLV3:WUS transgene at 10 days after germination (DAG) displayed a drastically enlarged SAM compared to wild-type seedlings of the same age (Figure 3C–D').
evidence: Observed phenotype shown in Figure 3C–D'

claim: Wild-type seedlings at 10 DAG express CLE40 in older leaf primordia and deeper regions of the vegetative SAM.
source: Wild-type seedlings at this stage express CLE40 in older leaf primordia and deeper regions of the vegetative SAM (Figure 3E–E').
evidence: Observed expression pattern from reporter line

claim: CLV3:WUS transgenic seedlings do not initiate lateral organs from the expanded meristem, and CLE40 expression is confined to the cotyledons.
source: The CLV3:WUS transgenic seedlings do not initiate lateral organs from the expanded meristem, and CLE40 expression is confined to the cotyledons (Figure 3F–F').
evidence: Observed phenotype and expression pattern from reporter line

claim: CLE40 is lacking in the deeper regions of the vegetative SAM in CLV3:WUS transgenic seedlings.
source: CLE40 is also lacking in the deeper regions of the vegetative SAM (Figure 3F').
evidence: Observed expression pattern from reporter line

claim: Either WUS itself or a WUS-dependent regulatory pathway represses CLE40 gene expression.
source: Thus. we conclude that either WUS itself or a WUS-dependent regulatory pathway represses CLE40 gene expression.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from CLV3:WUS misexpression and clv3-9 mutant data

claim: wus-7 mutants are developmentally delayed.
source: wus-7 mutants are developmentally delayed.
evidence: Observed phenotype of wus-7 mutants

claim: wus-7 mutants generate an IFM, but the FMs give rise to sterile flowers that lack inner organs.
source: Furthermore, wus-7 mutants generate an IFM, but the FMs give rise to sterile flowers that lack inner organs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Observed phenotype shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: At 5 WAG all wus-7 mutants expressed CLE40 in both the CZ and the OC of the IFM.
source: We introgressed the CLE40 reporter into wus-7 and found that at 5 WAG all wus-7 mutants expressed CLE40 in both the CZ and the OC of the IFM (Figure 3G–H', Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Observed expression pattern from reporter line in wus-7 background

claim: Similar to wild type, CLE40 is only weakly expressed in the young primordia of wus-7.
source: Similar to wild type, CLE40 is only weakly expressed in the young primordia of wus-7.
evidence: Observed expression pattern from reporter line

claim: A WUS-dependent pathway downregulates CLE40 in the centre of the IFM during normal development.
source: Therefore, we conclude that a WUS-dependent pathway downregulates CLE40 in the centre of the IFM during normal development.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from wus-7 mutant expression data

claim: Both CLV1:CLV1-GFP and BAM1:BAM1-GFP reporter lines rescued the shoot phenotype in clv1-101 and bam1-3;clv1-20 mutant backgrounds, respectively.
source: Both reporter lines rescued the shoot phenotype in a clv1-101 and bam1-3;clv1-20 mutant background, respectively.
evidence: Functional complementation demonstrated by phenotypic rescue

claim: The CLV1 reporter line showed the same expression pattern in the shoot compared to a previously published reporter line.
source: The CLV1 reporter line additionally showed the same expression pattern in the shoot compared to a previously published reporter line (Nimchuk et al., 2011; Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 3, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Comparison with previously published data from Nimchuk et al., 2011

claim: CLV1:CLV1-GFP is continuously expressed in deeper regions of the IFM comprising the OC, and in the meristem periphery where new FMs are initiating.
source: We observed dynamic changes of CLV1 expression during the different stages of flower primordia initiation. CLV1:CLV1-GFP is continuously expressed in deeper regions of the IFM comprising the OC, and in the meristem periphery where new FMs are initiating (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Observed expression pattern from CLV1:CLV1-GFP reporter line

claim: CLV1 is expressed strongly in cells of the L1 and L2 of incipient organ primordia (P-1, P0), and only in L2 at P1.
source: CLV1 is expressed strongly in cells of the L1 and L2 of incipient organ primordia (P-1, P0), and only in L2 at P1.
evidence: Observed expression pattern from reporter line

claim: P2 and P3 show only very faint CLV1 expression in the L1, but in stages from P4 to P6, CLV1 expression expands from the L3 into the L2 and L1.
source: P2 and P3 show only very faint expression in the L1, but in stages from P4 to P6, CLV1 expression expands from the L3 into the L2 and L1 (Figure 4, P1–P6, Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Observed expression pattern from reporter line

claim: The translational BAM1:BAM1-GFP reporter is expressed in the IFM, the FMs and in floral organs.
source: The translational BAM1:BAM1-GFP reporter is expressed in the IFM, the FMs and in floral organs (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C', Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–E').
evidence: Observed expression pattern from BAM1:BAM1-GFP reporter line

claim: In the IFM, BAM1 expression is found throughout the L1 layer of the meristem, and, at an elevated level, in L2 and L3 cells of the PZ, but not in the meristem centre around the OC, where CLV1 expression is detected.
source: In the IFM, expression is found throughout the L1 layer of the meristem, and, at an elevated level, in L2 and L3 cells of the PZ, but not in the meristem centre around the OC, where CLV1 expression is detected (Figure 5B and C, compare to Figure 4C).
evidence: Observed expression pattern from reporter line

claim: BAM1 is less expressed in the deeper regions of primordia from P6 onwards.
source: BAM1 is less expressed in the deeper regions of primordia from P6 onwards (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 3A'–E').
evidence: Observed expression pattern from reporter line

claim: BAM1 transcription was reported to be upregulated in the meristem centre in the absence of CLV3 or CLV1 signalling.
source: BAM1 transcription was reported to be upregulated in the meristem centre in the absence of CLV3 or CLV1 signalling (Nimchuk, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nimchuk, 2017

claim: Using the translational BAM1 reporter in the clv1-20 mutant background, BAM1 is now expressed in the meristem centre, similar to the pattern of CLV1 in the wild type, and BAM1 is upregulated in the L1 of the meristem.
source: Using our translational BAM1 reporter in the clv1-20 mutant background, we quantified and thereby confirmed that BAM1 is now expressed in the meristem centre, similar to the pattern of CLV1 in the wild type, and that BAM1 is upregulated in the L1 of the meristem.
evidence: Observed and quantified expression pattern from reporter line in clv1-20 background

claim: In a clv1-20 background BAM1 is absent in the peripheral region of the IFM and the L2.
source: Importantly, in a clv1-20 background BAM1 is absent in the peripheral region of the IFM and the L2 (Figure 5D–F, Figure 4—figure supplement 3F–J', Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Observed expression pattern from reporter line in clv1-20 background

claim: In the root meristem, the BAM1 receptor, but not CLV1, is required for CLE40-dependent root meristem development.
source: In the root meristem, we found that the BAM1 receptor, but not CLV1, is required for CLE40-dependent root meristem development, suggesting that CLE40 can act through BAM1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Root length assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: cle40-2 mutant IFMs reached 65% of the wild-type size.
source: While cle40-2 mutant IFMs reached 65% of the wild-type size, clv1-101 plants develop IFMs that were 140% wild-type size, whereas bam1-3;clv1-101 double mutant meristems reached 450% wild-type size, similar to those of clv3-9 mutants.
evidence: Quantitative meristem size measurements

claim: clv1-101 plants develop IFMs that were 140% wild-type size.
source: While cle40-2 mutant IFMs reached 65% of the wild-type size, clv1-101 plants develop IFMs that were 140% wild-type size, whereas bam1-3;clv1-101 double mutant meristems reached 450% wild-type size, similar to those of clv3-9 mutants.
evidence: Quantitative meristem size measurements

claim: bam1-3;clv1-101 double mutant meristems reached 450% wild-type size, similar to those of clv3-9 mutants.
source: While cle40-2 mutant IFMs reached 65% of the wild-type size, clv1-101 plants develop IFMs that were 140% wild-type size, whereas bam1-3;clv1-101 double mutant meristems reached 450% wild-type size, similar to those of clv3-9 mutants.
evidence: Quantitative meristem size measurements

claim: BAM1 can partially compensate for CLV1 function in the CLV3 signalling pathway when expressed in the meristem centre.
source: This supports the notion that BAM1 can partially compensate for CLV1 function in the CLV3 signalling pathway when expressed in the meristem centre (Figure 5F; Nimchuk et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by data and citation to Nimchuk et al., 2015

claim: The relationship between CLV1 and BAM1 is not symmetrical since CLV1 is expressed in a wild-typic pattern in bam1-3 mutants.
source: The relationship between CLV1 and BAM1 is not symmetrical since CLV1 is expressed in a wild-typic pattern in bam1-3 mutants (Figure 8—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Observed expression pattern from reporter line in bam1-3 background

claim: Meristem sizes of bam1-3 mutants reached 70% of the wild type.
source: Meristem sizes of bam1-3 mutants reached 70% of the wild type, and double mutants of cle40-2;bam1-3 did not differ significantly.
evidence: Quantitative meristem size measurements

claim: Double mutants of cle40-2;bam1-3 did not differ significantly from bam1-3 single mutants in meristem size.
source: Meristem sizes of bam1-3 mutants reached 70% of the wild type, and double mutants of cle40-2;bam1-3 did not differ significantly.
evidence: Quantitative meristem size measurements

claim: Double mutants of cle40-2;clv1-101 developed like the clv1-101 single mutant, indicating an epistatic relationship.
source: However, double mutants of cle40-2;clv1-101 developed like the clv1-101 single mutant, indicating an epistatic relationship.
evidence: Observed phenotype indicating genetic epistasis

claim: Both clv1-101 and bam1-3 mutants lack BAM1 function in the meristem periphery where CLE40 is highly expressed.
source: Importantly, both clv1-101 and bam1-3 mutants lack BAM1 function in the meristem periphery (Figure 5F), where also CLE40 is highly expressed, which could explain the observed epistatic relationships of cle40-2 with both clv1-101 and bam1-3.
evidence: Inference from expression patterns and genetic data

claim: Generation of larger IFMs and FMs in different mutants was negatively correlated with leaf size.
source: We also noted that generation of larger IFMs and FMs in different mutants was negatively correlated with leaf size, which we cannot explain so far (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observed correlation from phenotypic measurements

claim: Compared to wild type, the WUS expression domain was laterally strongly expanded in both clv3-9 and clv1-101.
source: Compared to wild type, the WUS expression domain was laterally strongly expanded in both clv3-9 and clv1-101.
evidence: Observed from WUS:NLS-GFP reporter line

claim: WUS signal extended into the L1 layer of clv1-101, albeit in a patchy pattern.
source: Interestingly, WUS signal extended also into the L1 layer of clv1-101, albeit in a patchy pattern (Figure 7A–C' and F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Observed from WUS:NLS-GFP reporter line in clv1-101 background

claim: BAM1 was expressed at a higher level in the L1 layer of clv1 mutants.
source: Also noteworthy is that BAM1 was expressed at a higher level in the L1 layer of clv1 mutants.
evidence: Observed from BAM1 reporter line in clv1 background

claim: cle40-2 mutants showed a reduction in the number of WUS-expressing cells down to ~50% wild-type levels.
source: cle40-2 mutants showed a reduction in the number of WUS-expressing cells down to ~50% wild-type levels (Figure 7D–D' and F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Quantitative cell counting from WUS reporter line

claim: WUS remained expressed in the centre of the meristem in cle40-2 mutants, but was found in a narrow domain.
source: Importantly, WUS remained expressed in the centre of the meristem, but was found in a narrow domain.
evidence: Observed from WUS reporter line in cle40-2 background

claim: In bam1-3 mutants, the WUS domain was similarly reduced as in cle40-2, and WUS expression focussed in the meristem centre.
source: In bam1-3 mutants, the WUS domain was similarly reduced as in cle40-2, and WUS expression focussed in the meristem centre (Figure 7E, E' and F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Observed from WUS reporter line in bam1-3 background

claim: Both clv3-9 and clv1-101 mutants express WUS in a laterally expanded domain.
source: In contrast, both clv3-9 and clv1-101 mutants express WUS in a laterally expanded domain (Figure 7B' and C', Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Observed from WUS reporter line in mutant backgrounds

claim: The CLE40-BAM1-WUS interaction establishes a new negative feedback loop.
source: To integrate our finding that CLE40 expression is repressed by WUS activity with the observation that WUS, in turn, is promoted by CLE40 signalling, we hypothesize that the CLE40-BAM1-WUS interaction establishes a new negative feedback loop.
evidence: Hypothesis based on integration of multiple experimental observations

claim: The CLE40-BAM1-WUS negative feedback loop acts in the meristem periphery, while the CLV3-CLV1-WUS negative feedback loop acts in the meristem centre along the apical-basal axis.
source: The CLE40-BAM1-WUS negative feedback loop acts in the meristem periphery, while the CLV3-CLV1-WUS negative feedback loop acts in the meristem centre along the apical-basal axis.
evidence: Conclusion from expression patterns and genetic data

claim: Both pathways act in parallel during development to regulate the size of the WUS expression domain in the meristem.
source: Both pathways act in parallel during development to regulate the size of the WUS expression domain in the meristem, possibly by perceiving input signals from two different regions, the CZ and the PZ, of the meristem.
evidence: Conclusion from genetic and expression data

claim: Meristems of cle40-2 and bam1-3 mutants were slightly reduced in width, and strongly reduced in height, resulting in reduced σ in comparison to Col-0.
source: In young IFMs at 4–5 WAG, when inflorescence stems were approximately 5–8 cm long, meristems of cle40-2 and bam1-3 mutants were slightly reduced in width, and strongly reduced in height, resulting in reduced σ in comparison to Col-0 (Figure 7G, Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Quantitative measurements of meristem dimensions

claim: Meristems of clv1-101 and clv3-9 mutants were similar in width to wild type, but strongly increased in height, giving high σ values.
source: Meristems of clv1-101 and clv3-9 mutants were similar in width to wild type, but strongly increased in height, giving high σ values (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Quantitative measurements of meristem dimensions

claim: CLV3-CLV1 signalling mostly restricts meristem growth along the apical-basal axis, while CLE40-BAM1 signalling promotes meristem growth along both axes.
source: This indicates that CLV3-CLV1 signalling mostly restricts meristem growth along the apical-basal axis, while CLE40-BAM1 signalling promotes meristem growth along both axes.
evidence: Conclusion from meristem shape analysis

claim: CLV3 signals from the CZ via CLV1 in the meristem centre to confine WUS expression to the OC.
source: CLV3 signals from the CZ via CLV1 in the meristem centre to confine WUS expression to the OC.
evidence: Established model from previous studies

claim: The diffusion of WUS protein along the apical-basal axis towards the meristem tip establishes the CZ and activates CLV3 expression as a feedback signal.
source: The diffusion of WUS protein along the apical-basal axis towards the meristem tip establishes the CZ and activates CLV3 expression as a feedback signal.
evidence: Established model from previous studies

claim: The PZ generates CLE40 as a short-range or autocrine signal that acts through BAM1 in the meristem periphery.
source: We now propose that the PZ generates CLE40 as a short-range or autocrine signal that acts through BAM1 in the meristem periphery.
evidence: Proposed model based on expression patterns and genetic data

claim: Since BAM1 and WUS expression does not overlap, a diffusible factor that relies on CLE40-BAM1 and acts from the PZ to promote WUS expression is postulated.
source: Since BAM1 and WUS expression does not overlap, we postulate the generation of a diffusible factor that relies on CLE40-BAM1 and acts from the PZ to promote WUS expression.
evidence: Hypothesis based on non-overlapping expression patterns

claim: WUS represses CLE40 expression from the OC, thus establishing a second negative feedback regulation.
source: WUS, in turn, represses CLE40 expression from the OC, thus establishing a second negative feedback regulation.
evidence: Conclusion from WUS misexpression and wus mutant data

claim: The two intertwined pathways serve to adjust WUS activity in the OC and incorporate information on the actual size of the stem cell domain, via CLV3-CLV1, and the growth requirements from the PZ via CLE40-BAM1.
source: Together, the two intertwined pathways serve to adjust WUS activity in the OC and incorporate information on the actual size of the stem cell domain, via CLV3-CLV1, and the growth requirements from the PZ via CLE40-BAM1.
evidence: Proposed model integrating all findings

claim: IFM size is reduced in cle40 mutants, indicating that CLE40 signalling promotes meristem size.
source: Here, we analysed the function of CLE40 in shoot development of Arabidopsis and found that WUS expression in the OC is under positive control from the PZ due to the activity of a CLE40-BAM1 signalling pathway. IFM size is reduced in cle40 mutants, indicating that CLE40 signalling promotes meristem size.
evidence: Observed phenotype of cle40 mutants

claim: CLE40 is expressed in the PZ, late-stage FMs and differentiating organs.
source: Importantly, CLE40 is expressed in the PZ, late-stage FMs and differentiating organs.
evidence: Observed expression pattern from reporter line

claim: CLE40 expression is confined to meristematic tissues, but not in organ founder sites or in regions with high WUS activity, such as the OC and the CZ.
source: A common denominator for the complex and dynamic expression pattern is that CLE40 expression is confined to meristematic tissues, but not in organ founder sites or in regions with high WUS activity, such as the OC and the CZ.
evidence: Summary of observed expression patterns

claim: CLE40 expression, in contrast to CLV3, is negatively controlled in a WUS-dependent manner.
source: Both misexpression of WUS in the CLV3 domain (Figure 3F), studies of clv3 mutants with expanded stem cell domains (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and analysis of wus mutants (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 2) underpinned the notion that CLE40 expression, in contrast to CLV3, is negatively controlled in a WUS-dependent manner.
evidence: Multiple lines of experimental evidence

claim: The number of WUS-expressing cells in cle40 mutant IFMs is strongly reduced, indicating that CLE40 exerts its positive effects on IFM size by expanding the WUS expression domain.
source: Furthermore, we found that the number of WUS-expressing cells in cle40 mutant IFMs is strongly reduced, indicating that CLE40 exerts its positive effects on IFM size by expanding the WUS expression domain.
evidence: Quantitative cell counting data

claim: The antagonistic effects of Arabidopsis CLV3 and CLE40 on meristem size can only be compared to the antagonistic functions of MpCLE1 and MpCLE2 on the gametophytic meristems of M. polymorpha.
source: So far, the antagonistic effects of Arabidopsis CLV3 and CLE40 on meristem size can only be compared to the antagonistic functions of MpCLE1 and MpCLE2 on the gametophytic meristems of M. polymorpha, which signal through two distinct receptors, MpTDR and MpCLV1, respectively (Hata and Kyozuka, 2021).
evidence: Comparison with published data from Hata and Kyozuka, 2021

claim: By the complementation of clv3 mutants through expression of CLE40 from the CLV3 promoter, it was shown previously that CLE40 and CLV3 are able to activate the same downstream receptors.
source: By the complementation of clv3 mutants through expression of CLE40 from the CLV3 promoter, it was shown previously that CLE40 and CLV3 are able to activate the same downstream receptors (Hobe et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hobe et al., 2003

claim: CLV3 and CLV1 are expressed in partially overlapping domains in the meristem centre, while CLE40 and BAM1 are confined to the meristem periphery.
source: Our detailed analysis of candidate receptor expression patterns showed that CLV3 and CLV1 are expressed in partially overlapping domains in the meristem centre, while CLE40 and BAM1 are confined to the meristem periphery.
evidence: Observed expression patterns from reporter lines

claim: Like cle40 mutants, bam1 mutant IFMs are smaller and maintain a smaller WUS expression domain.
source: Like cle40 mutants, bam1 mutant IFMs are smaller and maintain a smaller WUS expression domain, supporting the notion that CLE40 and BAM1 comprise a signalling unit that increases meristem size by promoting WUS expression.
evidence: Observed phenotypes of bam1 mutants

claim: The antagonistic functions of the CLV3-CLV1 and CLE40-BAM1 pathways in the regulation of WUS are reflected in their complementary expression patterns.
source: The antagonistic functions of the CLV3-CLV1 and CLE40-BAM1 pathways in the regulation of WUS are reflected in their complementary expression patterns.
evidence: Inference from expression patterns and genetic data

claim: WUS has been previously shown to promote CLV3 levels in the CZ.
source: There is cross-regulation between these two signalling pathways at two levels: (1) WUS has been previously shown to promote CLV3 levels in the CZ, and we here show that WUS represses (directly or indirectly) CLE40 expression in the OC and in the CZ (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Established knowledge and new data

claim: CLV1 represses BAM1 expression in the OC, and thereby restricts BAM1 to the meristem periphery.
source: and (2) CLV1 represses BAM1 expression in the OC, and thereby restricts BAM1 to the meristem periphery (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: Observed from reporter line expression in clv1 mutants

claim: In clv1 mutants, BAM1 shifts from the meristem periphery to the OC, and the WUS domain laterally expands in the meristem centre.
source: In clv1 mutants, BAM1 shifts from the meristem periphery to the OC, and the WUS domain laterally expands in the meristem centre (Figures 5F and 7B').
evidence: Observed expression patterns in clv1 mutants

claim: BAM1 expression increases in the L1 in clv1 mutants, which could cause the observed irregular expression of WUS in the outermost cell layer of clv1 mutants.
source: Furthermore, BAM1 expression increases also in the L1, which could cause the observed irregular expression of WUS in the outermost cell layer of clv1 mutants.
evidence: Inference from expression patterns

claim: Despite the high-sequence similarity between CLV1 and BAM1, the expression of BAM1 in the OC is not sufficient to compensate for the loss of CLV1.
source: The role of BAM1 in the OC is not entirely clear: despite the high-sequence similarity between CLV1 and BAM1, the expression of BAM1 in the OC is not sufficient to compensate for the loss of CLV1 (Figure 5D–F, Nimchuk et al., 2015).
evidence: Observed phenotype and citation to Nimchuk et al., 2015

claim: In the OC, BAM1 appears to restrict WUS expression to some extent since clv1;bam1 double mutants reveal a drastically expanded IFM.
source: In the OC, BAM1 appears to restrict WUS expression to some extent since clv1;bam1 double mutants reveal a drastically expanded IFM (Deyoung and Clark, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Deyoung and Clark, 2008

claim: BAM1 in the absence of CLV1 may execute a dual function: to repress WUS in response to CLV3 in the OC as a substitute for CLV1 and simultaneously to promote WUS expression in the L1 in response to CLE40.
source: However, it is possible that BAM1 in the absence of CLV1 executes a dual function: to repress WUS in response to CLV3 in the OC as a substitute for CLV1 and simultaneously to promote WUS expression in the L1 in response to CLE40.
evidence: Hypothesis based on genetic and expression data

claim: The expression domains of CLE40 and its receptor BAM1 largely coincide, suggesting that CLE40 acts as an autocrine signal.
source: The expression domains of CLE40 and its receptor BAM1 largely coincide, suggesting that CLE40 acts as an autocrine signal.
evidence: Inference from overlapping expression patterns

claim: Protophloem sieve element differentiation in roots is inhibited by CLE45, which acts as an autocrine signal via BAM3.
source: Similarly, protophloem sieve element differentiation in roots is inhibited by CLE45, which acts as an autocrine signal via BAM3 (Kang and Hardtke, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kang and Hardtke, 2016

claim: A non-cell-autonomous signal X is postulated that is generated in the PZ due to CLE40-BAM1 signalling and diffuses towards the meristem centre to promote WUS expression.
source: Since WUS is not expressed in the same cells as BAM1, we have to postulate a non-cell-autonomous signal X that is generated in the PZ due to CLE40-BAM1 signalling and diffuses towards the meristem centre to promote WUS expression (Hohm et al., 2010).
evidence: Hypothesis based on non-overlapping expression patterns and citation to Hohm et al., 2010

claim: CLE40-BAM1 signalling from the PZ provides the necessary feedback signal that stimulates stem cell activity and thereby serves to replenish cells in the meristem for the initiation of new organs.
source: As a result, CLE40-BAM1 signalling from the PZ will provide the necessary feedback signal that stimulates stem cell activity and thereby serves to replenish cells in the meristem for the initiation of new organs.
evidence: Proposed model based on all findings

claim: The CLV3-CLV1 signalling pathway adopts the role of a necessary feedback signal that avoids an excessive stem cell production.
source: The CLV3-CLV1 signalling pathway then adopts the role of a necessary feedback signal that avoids an excessive stem cell production.
evidence: Proposed model based on established knowledge

claim: The previous model, which focussed mainly on the interaction of the CZ and the OC via the CLV3-CLV1-WUS negative feedback regulation, lacked any direct regulatory contribution from the PZ.
source: The two intertwined, antagonistically acting signalling pathways that we described here allow us to better understand the regulation of shoot meristem growth, development and shape. The previous model, which focussed mainly on the interaction of the CZ and the OC via the CLV3-CLV1-WUS negative feedback regulation, lacked any direct regulatory contribution from the PZ.
evidence: Critique of previous models

claim: EPFL peptides were shown to be expressed in the periphery and to restrict both CLV3 and WUS expression via ER.
source: EPFL peptides were shown to be expressed in the periphery and to restrict both CLV3 and WUS expression via ER (Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2021

claim: EPFL peptide expression is not reported to be feedback regulated from the OC or CZ, and the main function of the EPFL-ER pathway is to restrict overall meristem size.
source: However, EPFL peptide expression is not reported to be feedback regulated from the OC or CZ, and the main function of the EPFL-ER pathway is therefore to restrict overall meristem size (Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2021

claim: The second negative feedback loop controlled by CLE40 enables the meristem to fine-tune stem cell activities in response to fluctuating requirements for new cells during organ initiation.
source: The second negative feedback loop controlled by CLE40, which we uncovered here, enables the meristem to fine-tune stem cell activities in response to fluctuating requirements for new cells during organ initiation.
evidence: Proposed function based on all findings

claim: Due to the combined activities of CLV3 and CLE40, the OC (with WUS as a key player) can now record and compute information from both, the CZ and PZ.
source: Due to the combined activities of CLV3 and CLE40, the OC (with WUS as a key player) can now record and compute information from both, the CZ and PZ.
evidence: Proposed model integrating both pathways

claim: Weaker CLV3 signalling, indicating a reduction in the size of the CZ, induces preferential growth of the meristem along the apical-basal axis (increasing σ).
source: Weaker CLV3 signalling, indicating a reduction in the size of the CZ, induces preferential growth of the meristem along the apical-basal axis (increasing σ), while weaker CLE40 signals, reporting a smaller PZ, would decrease σ and flatten meristem shape.
evidence: Inference from meristem shape analysis

claim: Weaker CLE40 signals, reporting a smaller PZ, would decrease σ and flatten meristem shape.
source: Weaker CLV3 signalling, indicating a reduction in the size of the CZ, induces preferential growth of the meristem along the apical-basal axis (increasing σ), while weaker CLE40 signals, reporting a smaller PZ, would decrease σ and flatten meristem shape.
evidence: Inference from meristem shape analysis

claim: Different levels of CLV3 and CLE40 may contribute to the shape changes that are observed during early vegetative development or upon floral transition in Arabidopsis.
source: It will be intriguing to investigate if different levels of CLV3 and CLE40 also contribute to the shape changes that are observed during early vegetative development or upon floral transition in Arabidopsis.
evidence: Speculation about future research directions

claim: Many shoot-expressed CLE peptides are encoded in the genomes of maize, rice and barley, which could act analogously to CLV3 and CLE40 of Arabidopsis.
source: Many shoot-expressed CLE peptides are encoded in the genomes of maize, rice and barley, which could act analogously to CLV3 and CLE40 of Arabidopsis.
evidence: Speculation based on genomic information

claim: In grasses a CLE40-like, stem cell-promoting signalling pathway may be more active than a CLV3-like, stem cell-restricting pathway, which could contribute to the typical shape of cereal SAMs.
source: It is tempting to speculate that in grasses a CLE40-like, stem cell-promoting signalling pathway is more active than a CLV3-like, stem cell-restricting pathway. This could contribute to the typical shape of cereal SAMs, which are, compared to the dome-shaped SAM of dicotyledonous plants, extended along the apical-basal axis.
evidence: Speculation about evolutionary differences
